name: Lunfa — AI Chinese writing tutor
context: A university research group needed a production web app that helps Chinese learners self-correct without the AI simply giving away the answer.
role: Freelance full-stack developer · team of 2 · requirements through deployment
evidence: Delivered and deployed for a university research group; project completed and paid in full.
tagline: A chatbot that finds grammar mistakes in a learner's Chinese sentence, highlights them, and coaches the learner to fix it themselves — instead of handing over the answer.

media.alt: Lunfa chatbot highlighting a Chinese grammar error and coaching the learner to rewrite the sentence
media.caption: Guided correction — highlight the error, explain the rule, then ask the learner to try again.

media.alt: Lunfa sign-in screen with email and Google authentication options
media.caption: Production authentication flow with email and Google sign-in.

flow.label: USER INPUT
flow.desc: Learner types a sentence in Chinese (HSK 1–4 level).

flow.label: AI ANALYZE
flow.desc: Gemini 2.5 Flash evaluates the sentence against a grammar rulebook.
flow.challenge: The AI sometimes returns broken JSON — control characters inside string values crash the parser.
flow.fix: A ~3,000-word system prompt pins the grammar rules + a strict output schema, with responseMimeType=JSON. On top of that, a 3-layer guard: normal parse → sanitize + regex-extract the JSON → safe fallback message. Malformed responses can fall back to a safe message without abandoning the conversation.

flow.label: HIGHLIGHT
flow.desc: Wrong words are painted red inside the original sentence.
flow.challenge: Highlighting the exact wrong word without matching a shorter substring elsewhere.
flow.fix: Build a dynamic split regex with error words sorted by length (longest first), then render each segment separately so only the real mistakes light up.

flow.label: SELF-CORRECT
flow.desc: The learner gets reason + correct structure + a prompt, and rewrites it themselves.
flow.challenge: Vertex AI requires the chat history to start with a 'user' role, and long history blows the token limit.
flow.fix: shift() off any leading non-user message and keep only the last 10 turns — pedagogy stays intact (never give the answer) while staying inside limits.

flow.label: MASTERED
flow.desc: Correct sentence accepted. Conversation auto-titled by Gemini and saved to MongoDB.

title: Help the learner find the answer.
subtitle: An AI writing tutor designed around self-correction.
summary: A delivered Chinese-writing tutor that highlights mistakes and guides a learner to correct them, with structured AI responses and safe fallbacks.
lessons: The learning experience determines the AI contract: guide the learner rather than reveal the answer.
Structured output still needs validation, recovery and a safe experience when the model fails.
limitations: Work was delivered to a university research group by a team of two. User counts and measured learning outcomes are not available.
Screenshots document the delivered interface; current live-site availability may change.

name: SSTC warranty operations platform
context: At the R&D and Service Center of SSTC Technology JSC, independently developed the warranty operations source from customer chat intake through shipping, warehouse reconciliation, inspection and return workflows.
role: Backend Developer Intern · Sole developer from requirements and data design through implementation, testing and handover
evidence: 29-state workflow engine · 57 versioned schema migrations · 800+ automated test methods in source · last documented full verification: 805 tests · handed over to SSTC R&D Center.
tagline: A workflow-heavy Spring Boot platform that keeps business decisions deterministic while coordinating customer intake, shipment tracking, warehouse evidence, technical inspection and returns.

media.alt: SSTC customer warranty chat showing intake progress and serial verification
media.caption: Customer intake — guided serial verification with a six-step progress indicator.

media.alt: SSTC warehouse receiving workspace for shipment scanning and reconciliation
media.caption: Warehouse receiving — scan shipment labels, reconcile expected and observed components, and preserve evidence.

media.alt: SSTC technical inspection workspace recording warranty findings
media.caption: Technical inspection — role-controlled findings and auditable approve or reject decisions.

media.alt: SSTC customer ticket lookup page with masked personal details
media.caption: Customer tracking — token-gated lookup with masked personal information.

accessNote: Company project · source repository is not publicly linked · no production data is included

architecture.label: Backend system map
architecture.status: Complete source handover · production data excluded

flow.label: CHAT INTAKE
flow.desc: The customer describes the warranty request naturally; the bot extracts intent and product clues without forcing a rigid form.
flow.challenge: An LLM is useful for understanding language, but it must never decide whether a product exists, is still covered, or deserves a ticket.
flow.fix: Claude is isolated behind an AiOrchestrator interface and only returns intent, confirmation and extracted fields. PII-bearing steps stay on local rules, and any timeout or malformed AI response falls back through Resilience4j to the deterministic mock engine.

flow.label: VERIFY SERIAL
flow.desc: The backend looks up the serial in PostgreSQL, reads the authoritative product identity and asks the customer to confirm it.
flow.challenge: Catalog values can be corrected later, but an issued warranty ticket must preserve exactly what was accepted at intake.
flow.fix: Serial-first verification reads warranty and product identity from relational data, then snapshots description, model, SKU, product number and serial onto the ticket while retaining the component foreign key.

flow.label: COLLECT PROOF
flow.desc: The bot gathers the issue, 1–5 condition photos, contact details, Zalo phone and pickup address, skipping fields already known.

flow.label: CREATE TICKET
flow.desc: A confirmed intake becomes a ticket with an atomic daily code such as NS-YYYYMMDD-000001.
flow.challenge: Rapid retries and duplicate messages can otherwise create duplicate tickets, active sessions or ticket codes.
flow.fix: Client-message idempotency, optimistic locking, database uniqueness constraints and an atomic ticket-code sequence keep concurrent turns consistent. External AI and shipping calls are kept outside long database transactions.

flow.label: SHIP & RECEIVE
flow.desc: A provider abstraction creates and tracks shipments; warehouse staff scan labels, reconcile received components and retain evidence.
flow.challenge: A shipping outage must not roll back or lose a warranty request that was already accepted.
flow.fix: Ticket creation and shipping application use separate short transactions. Idempotency and a shipping-state ledger make retries and out-of-order provider events recoverable.

flow.label: INSPECT & RETURN
flow.desc: Role-controlled inspection, manager decisions, customer consent and return fulfillment remain traceable through append-only audit and evidence records.

title: Warranty operations, engineered end to end.
subtitle: A backend that makes the business rules explicit.
summary: From customer intake to inspection and returns: a Spring Boot workflow where the backend owns every business decision.
lessons: A language model can interpret a request without owning the business decision.
Make duplicate delivery and partial failure part of the design, rather than exceptions to it.
limitations: Company source and production data are not public. This case study describes the delivered design, not a live production system.
The 29 states, 57 migrations and documented 805-test run refer to the final handover described in the portfolio records; implementation count and documented execution are distinct measures.

name: UniHub Workshop — event lifecycle platform
context: A university event platform needed registration, payment and door check-in to remain dependable during traffic spikes and unreliable venue Wi-Fi.
role: Team of 2 · admin panel, offline check-in, Redis, rate limiting, UI/UX and database design
evidence: The Spring Boot backend and React frontend were built and run against an isolated PostgreSQL database. These screenshots show the actual interface with synthetic data; login, attendee search and manual check-in were verified through the browser.
tagline: Digitizes a university's 'skills & career week': student registers → pays by QR → gets an emailed QR ticket → staff scans it at the door, even with no WiFi. Built to survive a real traffic spike.
note: K6 spike scenario authored for up to 12,000 virtual users.

flow.label: REGISTER
flow.desc: Student claims a seat for a workshop.
flow.challenge: A registration traffic spike can oversell seats when requests read the same remaining capacity.
flow.fix: Optimistic locking (@Version): when two transactions read version=1, only one commits — the other gets OptimisticLockException and is told the seat is gone. A unique (user_id, workshop_id) constraint blocks double-submits, and a 2-tier Redis rate limit (5 req/10s per IP) shields the endpoint.

flow.label: QR PAYMENT
flow.desc: Pays via the SePay QR gateway; a webhook confirms asynchronously.
flow.challenge: If the payment gateway hangs, it could exhaust the thread pool and take the whole system down.
flow.fix: A Resilience4j circuit breaker trips OPEN after repeated timeouts → fail-fast instead of piling up blocked threads.

flow.label: EMAIL TICKET
flow.desc: A QR-coded ticket is emailed asynchronously via Spring events + @Async, so the API responds instantly.

flow.label: OFFLINE CHECK-IN
flow.desc: Staff scan tickets at the venue through a PWA.
flow.challenge: The auditorium WiFi drops in the middle of the event.
flow.fix: A service worker caches the app shell. The frontend stores cached workshop/attendee lists and pending check-ins in localStorage, then retries queued updates when the browser returns online.

flow.label: ATTENDED
flow.desc: Check-in recorded. SeatReleaseJob frees expired PENDING tickets back to the pool.

title: One event. Every edge case.
subtitle: Registration, payment and check-in as one dependable journey.
summary: Workshop registration that considers competing requests, asynchronous payments and a venue with unreliable Wi-Fi.
lessons: The interesting part of a registration system is what happens when requests compete.
Offline support requires a reconciliation strategy, not only a cached screen.
limitations: The interactive model is an illustration in the browser, not a connection to the project backend.
A K6 scenario targeting up to 12,000 virtual users was authored. No measured latency, throughput or error-rate result is claimed here.
Camera scanning, offline-to-online reconciliation and live payment/email integrations were not exercised in this local capture. Redis used an in-memory fallback in this environment.

name: Online Auction Platform
context: A marketplace needed concurrent bidding, anti-sniping and the buyer–seller handoff after an auction to behave as one coherent system.
role: Team of 2 · requirements, UI/UX, database design, bidder/seller systems, chat and order tracking
evidence: 17-table relational schema · 50+ documented endpoints · 6 route groups · 3 user roles.
tagline: A full marketplace: bidders bid, sellers list, admins govern. Auto-bid, Buy Now, anti-sniping, a 4-step post-auction payment flow, buyer–seller chat and reputation — all kept correct under concurrent bids.
note: 17-table schema · 50+ documented endpoints · 6 route groups · 3 roles.

flow.label: LISTED
flow.desc: Seller posts a product with a WYSIWYG editor and multi-image upload to Cloudinary.

flow.label: BIDDING
flow.desc: Bidders place manual bids or set an auto-bid ceiling.
flow.challenge: Many people bid the same product at the same millisecond → price race condition.
flow.fix: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE takes a row-level lock inside a transaction, so only one bid is processed per product at a time. Auto-bid is its own 3-branch state machine (raise ceiling / lose to old ceiling / beat old bidder), all in one transaction.

flow.label: ANTI-SNIPE
flow.desc: Guards against last-second sniping.
flow.challenge: Snipers bid in the final seconds to deny others a counter-bid.
flow.fix: If time-remaining < 5 minutes when a bid lands, end_at is pushed +10 minutes — the snipe strategy stops working.

flow.label: WON
flow.desc: Auction closes. A node-cron job runs every minute to detect ended auctions and fire 6 kinds of notification email.

flow.label: PAID → SHIPPED
flow.desc: Buyer uploads payment proof, seller confirms shipping, buyer confirms receipt.
flow.challenge: Sending email must never block the API response.
flow.fix: Email is dispatched without awaiting completion in the request, with rejection handling. This reduces request-path waiting; a durable queue or transactional outbox would be needed for stronger delivery guarantees across process failures.

flow.label: RATED
flow.desc: Both sides leave +/- reputation. Denormalized current_price & bid_count keep listing queries fast.

title: Keep the bidding fair.
subtitle: Concurrency and settlement in one relational model.
summary: A marketplace with concurrent bidding, anti-sniping and a traceable buyer-seller handoff.
lessons: The bid, current price and winner must be decided within a consistent transaction.
A fast response and guaranteed background delivery are separate design problems.
limitations: Email calls were dispatched outside the request wait path; this alone does not guarantee delivery after a process failure.
A durable queue or transactional outbox is a possible next step when delivery guarantees are required.

name: Coffee Shop POS & Management
context: A real coffee shop needed staff ordering, role-specific operations and management reporting in one daily-use system.
role: Team of 4 · owned the POS/order module, system UI/UX and requirements analysis
evidence: Deployed for daily use at a GUTA coffee shop; no current usage metrics are claimed.
tagline: A role-based system for a real coffee shop (GUTA): staff take orders on a POS, managers watch revenue analytics, HR runs shift scheduling. Admin / Manager / Staff each get their own surface.

flow.label: BROWSE
flow.desc: Staff browse drinks by category — the POS module I built end-to-end.

flow.label: CART
flow.desc: Real-time cart with per-item notes (preset tags + free text).

flow.label: CHECKOUT
flow.desc: A 3-step checkout: Summary → Transfer → Success.
flow.challenge: Circular foreign keys: orders.payment_id → payment and payment.order_id → orders.
flow.fix: DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED constraints let both rows be inserted inside the same transaction without a chicken-and-egg failure.

flow.label: SUCCESS
flow.desc: Order completed and persisted; receipt issued.

flow.label: DASHBOARD
flow.desc: Managers see revenue-by-hour, peak hours and period-over-period comparisons.
flow.challenge: Heavy analytics queries on the manager dashboard, plus keeping staff out of it.
flow.fix: CTEs build the revenue aggregates, Promise.all() runs 9 analytics queries in parallel, and values are cast ::int/::bigint in SQL to avoid string/number bugs in JS. RBAC: a RequireAuth guard on the client + an authorize(...roles) middleware factory on the server.

title: Software for the everyday rush.
subtitle: A POS flow built around the people behind the counter.
summary: Owned the POS and order module, requirements analysis and system UI for a coffee-shop management product.
lessons: Checkout needs a clear user journey and an equally clear transaction boundary.
Separate staff tasks from manager tasks in both the interface and server authorization.
limitations: Team of four. My ownership was the POS/order module, system UI/UX and requirements analysis.
The project was deployed for use at a GUTA coffee shop; no current usage analytics or uptime claim is made.

name: HomestayDorm — rental operations
context: A multi-branch rental workflow needed to track each resident from initial inquiry through viewing, deposit, contract and move-out.
role: Team of 4 · registration module, Prisma schema, UI/UX and requirements analysis
evidence: 15+ data models · bed-level availability · 6-state registration workflow.
tagline: Runs a dorm/rental business down to the individual bed: intake → consult → viewing → deposit → contract → move-out & reconciliation. Multi-branch, 3 roles, built fullstack on Next.js Server Actions (no separate REST API).

flow.label: DRAFT → CONSULT
flow.desc: The registration ticket I owned: a 6-state machine (DRAFT → CONSULTING → WAITING_VIEW → WAITLIST → COMPLETED / CANCELLED).
flow.challenge: Manage availability at bed granularity, not just per room.
flow.fix: Modeled Room → Bed (1-to-N), each bed with its own status (AVAILABLE / OCCUPIED / DEPOSITED / MAINTENANCE) and price — so a room can be rented whole or shared.

flow.label: VIEWING
flow.desc: A viewing appointment is scheduled off the registration ticket.

flow.label: DEPOSIT → CONTRACT
flow.desc: Deposit taken, then a contract is signed per bed.
flow.challenge: If admin changes a bed's price later, old contracts must not change.
flow.fix: Price-snapshot pattern: ContractBedDetail stores priceAtSigning at signing time, fully decoupled from future price edits.

flow.label: RETURN
flow.desc: Move-out and reconciliation.
flow.challenge: Return-room has 10+ possible states.
flow.fix: A clearly-defined ReturnRoomTicketStatus enum, with every transition validated at the Server Action layer.

title: Model the business down to the bed.
subtitle: Rental operations with explicit states and stable contracts.
summary: Bed-level allocation and a registration workflow connecting inquiries, appointments, deposits and contracts.
lessons: Model inventory at the level where the business actually makes allocation decisions.
A signed contract must preserve the accepted price even when the catalog changes.
limitations: Team of four. My scope was the registration module, Prisma schema, UI/UX and requirements analysis.
This case study describes project implementation, not measured commercial operation.

name: PetCareX — vet clinic management
context: A veterinary clinic system needed bookings, examinations, prescriptions, billing and customer benefits to work across multiple roles and branches.
role: Team of 4 · sole frontend and backend implementer; teammates handled design
evidence: 5 roles · 9 route groups · customer and staff layouts · parameterized raw SQL without an ORM.
tagline: A multi-branch veterinary clinic system — booking, examination, prescriptions, billing, subscription packages and loyalty points. I was the sole developer (frontend + backend) in a 4-person team.
note: 5 roles · 9 route groups · dual layout (customer vs staff) · raw SQL, no ORM.

flow.label: BOOK
flow.desc: Customer books an exam / vaccination / spa slot.
flow.challenge: Two customers book the same doctor for the same time slot.
flow.fix: A conflict-detection query checks existing doctor appointments before insertion and returns a validation error for a known clash. This precheck alone does not guarantee correctness under simultaneous requests; database coordination is a separate requirement.

flow.label: CONFIRM
flow.desc: Front desk confirms (PENDING → WAITING).

flow.label: EXAM
flow.desc: Doctor examines the pet and records a diagnosis.

flow.label: PRESCRIBE → INVOICE
flow.desc: Prescription written, invoice generated automatically.
flow.challenge: Finishing an exam must atomically update status, write the prescription and create a correct invoice.
flow.fix: One PostgreSQL transaction (BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK) updates the visit, inserts the prescription and creates the invoice (exam fee + drug fee), then moves it to WAITING_PAYMENT. Parameterized $1,$2 queries keep raw SQL injection-safe.

flow.label: PAID
flow.desc: Payment recorded → loyalty points added, active service packages decremented per use.

title: Keep clinical operations connected.
subtitle: From appointment to prescription, invoice and payment.
summary: Implemented the frontend and backend of a multi-role veterinary clinic system with parameterized SQL and transactional updates.
lessons: An exam completion is a business transaction spanning several tables, not a collection of unrelated updates.
A booking precheck improves validation but needs database-level coordination to prove correctness under concurrency.
limitations: The described booking conflict precheck does not by itself prove race-free double-booking prevention.
Sole frontend/backend implementer within a four-person team; teammates handled design.

name: Melodix — Android music streaming
context: A three-role music app needed resilient playback, offline listening and an artist workflow on top of a shared Supabase backend.
role: Team of 4 · artist module, detail/search/share/profile flows, UI/UX and database co-design
evidence: 12 repositories · 14 API services · 10+ ViewModels · online and offline playback paths.
tagline: A Spotify-style Android app with 3 roles (User / Artist / Admin): background playback, offline download, synced lyrics, Supabase backend. MVVM with 12 repositories, 14 API services, 10+ ViewModels.

flow.label: PLAY
flow.desc: User taps a song; playback starts through ExoPlayer.
flow.challenge: The JWT can expire mid-session while the user is browsing.
flow.fix: An OkHttp Authenticator catches 401s, silently refreshes the token and retries the original request — transparent to the UI layer. A play only counts after 15 continuous seconds, to avoid counting brief starts as full plays.

flow.label: BACKGROUND
flow.desc: Music keeps playing when the app is backgrounded, with a media notification.
flow.challenge: Android can kill the process and stop playback.
flow.fix: A Foreground Service and MediaSession support playback and media controls while the app is backgrounded. START_STICKY provides a restart strategy, subject to Android lifecycle restrictions and user-initiated stopping.

flow.label: DOWNLOAD
flow.desc: Songs are downloaded for offline listening via WorkManager.
flow.challenge: Scoped Storage changed how files are written on Android 10+.
flow.fix: Branch by SDK version — Android 10+ uses the MediaStore API (ContentResolver), 9- uses the file system directly. Either way, metadata lands in Room DB.

flow.label: OFFLINE
flow.desc: Tracks play from the local Room library with no network.

title: Music beyond the foreground.
subtitle: An Android product with online and offline listening paths.
summary: Artist tools, discovery and detail flows in a Java Android app with MVVM and a shared Supabase backend.
lessons: Playback needs lifecycle-aware state and recovery, not only an audio player component.
A repository boundary helps UI flows share data without sharing every implementation detail.
limitations: Foreground services support background playback but do not guarantee the app can never be stopped.
My scope covered the artist module, detail/search/share/profile flows, UI/UX and database co-design.
